content: The system was designed to collect data and ensure that medical information is accessible within both the civil health system and prison health services. A financial sustainability plan was established, where the prison administration assumed responsibility for the procurement of first-line tuberculosis (TB) medications. Meanwhile, antiretroviral therapy (ART), opioid agonist maintenance therapy (OAMT), and medical equipment are funded by national programs for HIV and drug use, the Global Fund, and various donors. Key factors enabling the implementation of an integrated, patient-centered model of care for TB, HIV, and OAMT in prisons included strong political commitment and a supportive legal framework. This ensured equivalent care for incarcerated individuals through the training of prison medical staff to deliver integrated care and the use of shared electronic systems for recording and reporting. Constructive dialogue and collaboration with civil society organizations also helped to overcome barriers to accessing care and treatment, as well as to address gaps in the treatment cascade. To create an environment conducive to people-centered care, programs in collaboration with stakeholders should support the expansion of financing models that promote integrated care and incentivize the provision of comprehensive services as part of national health financing strategies. Legislation and funding should also enable the engagement of peer supporters with lived experience of relevant health conditions to deliver people-centered TB care. Measures to address stigma and discrimination include capacity building for civil society organizations, targeted advocacy for decriminalizing drug use in line with UN and WHO recommendations, and strengthening linkages with prison services to ensure equitable access to comprehensive care for TB and comorbidities, including harm reduction services. Meaningful engagement of civil society and affected communities is essential at all stages of planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of people-centered services for TB and comorbidities. Strategies include involving these groups in policy formulation, planning, and operational research, expanding community-based interventions for TB prevention and care, and empowering communities to advocate for high-quality, non-discriminatory care and resource availability. In Peru, where multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) is a significant burden, the national TB program introduced an intervention to address the mental health comorbidities often experienced by TB patients, such as anxiety and depression. This initiative involved training healthcare workers in mental health interventions based on WHO guidelines and integrating psychologists into multidisciplinary TB teams. These teams collaboratively assessed the needs of TB patients and provided specialist care for both TB and mental health conditions. Broader psychosocial care, including group psychotherapy and activities like yoga and music therapy, was also offered to improve mental health and reduce stigma. Routine data from Lima North showed a reduction in loss-to-follow-up rates for TB treatment from 10% to 2% for drug-susceptible TB and from 42% to 4% for drug-resistant TB between 2015 and 2021. In Mexico, collaborative action on TB and diabetes was introduced in 2012, recognizing the higher risk of TB among people with diabetes. Bidirectional screening for TB in diabetes patients and vice versa was implemented, with treatment for both conditions provided in the same primary care clinic. Weekly counseling sessions promoted adherence to treatment, healthy diets, and physical activity. National TB guidelines were updated to include diabetes management, and strategies for scaling up collaborative care included training healthcare workers, regular meetings between TB and diabetes program representatives, and the introduction of joint indicators to monitor progress. In Pakistan, where smoking prevalence among adults is high, behavioral support for smoking cessation was integrated into TB care. This initiative aimed to address the significant impact of smoking on TB outcomes and included counseling and support for patients to quit smoking as part of their TB treatment plan.
